_about: Passages that tell or repeat the same material. Differences are noted so that they can be compared; a difference is not treated as a contradiction.

entries.note: The census of David. Samuel says the Lord moved David to number the people; Chronicles says Satan did. Both agree that David sinned and that the threshing floor of Araunah (Ornan) became the site of the altar.
God's covenant with David through Nathan. The Chronicles version is shorter and omits the clause about David's punishment for wrongdoing.
David is anointed king over all Israel and takes Jerusalem.
The bringing of the ark to Jerusalem. Chronicles gives much more attention to the Levites and the liturgy.
Solomon's dream at Gibeon and his request for wisdom.
The building and dedication of the Temple. Chronicles is more interested in the cult and the Levites.
The visit of the queen of Sheba.
Sennacherib's invasion of Judah and Hezekiah's deliverance. Isaiah repeats the Kings narrative almost word for word, and omits Hezekiah's tribute (2 Kings 18:14-16).
Hezekiah's illness and the envoys from Babylon. Isaiah adds Hezekiah's psalm (38:9-20).
The fall of Jerusalem. Jeremiah 52 is very close to the end of 2 Kings, and shows that the book of Jeremiah ends with the same history.
David's song of deliverance, found in both Samuel and the Psalter with small differences in wording.
The same psalm with small differences, notably the use of the divine name: 'the Lord' in Psalm 14, 'God' in Psalm 53.
Psalm 70 is nearly identical to the end of Psalm 40.
Psalm 108 joins together part of Psalm 57 and part of Psalm 60.
A portion of David's thanksgiving song in Chronicles, close to Psalm 96.
The Ten Commandments. The Sabbath commandment differs in its reason: creation in Exodus, the exodus from Egypt in Deuteronomy.
Two lists of clean and unclean animals.
The release of Hebrew slaves. Deuteronomy also includes women and adds a provision for generosity at release.
Two accounts of creation in Genesis. The first is a seven-day structure; the second is a narrative that begins with the man and the garden.
Three accounts of the patriarch passing off his wife as his sister. Scholars debate whether these are separate events or variants of one tradition.
Boundary lists of the tribes. Compare with the lists of towns in Judges and Chronicles.
The opening genealogies of Chronicles condense lists from Genesis.
The list of those who returned from exile, with minor differences in numbers.
The preaching of John the Baptist and the baptism of Jesus.
The temptation of Jesus in the wilderness. Matthew and Luke give the three temptations in a different order.
The Sermon on the Mount in Matthew and the shorter Sermon on the Plain in Luke, with many sayings in common.
The Beatitudes. Matthew gives nine, spiritualised ('poor in spirit'); Luke gives four blessings and four woes in the second person.
The Lord's Prayer. Matthew's form is the longer one and the one used in the liturgy.
The calming of the storm.
The parable of the sower and its explanation.
The feeding of the five thousand, the only miracle of Jesus told in all four Gospels.
The feeding of the four thousand.
Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi. Only Matthew has the words to Peter about the keys and the rock (16:17-19).
The Transfiguration.
The rich young man.
The entry into Jerusalem.
The parable of the wicked tenants.
The Olivet discourse on the destruction of the Temple and the end.
The Last Supper and the words over the bread and the cup. Paul's is the earliest written account.
Gethsemane.
The crucifixion. Each Gospel records different words of Jesus from the cross.
The empty tomb and the first appearances.
The final commission and the ascension. Mark 16:9-20 is a longer ending absent from the oldest manuscripts.

The two genealogies of Jesus. Matthew goes from Abraham through David's son Solomon; Luke goes back through David's son Nathan to Adam. Ancient and modern interpreters explain the differences in several ways.
The two infancy narratives. Luke is told mostly from Mary's perspective and Matthew from Joseph's.
The thanksgiving to the Father: the 'Johannine thunderbolt' in the synoptic tradition.
Three accounts of Paul's conversion in Acts, with differences in what his companions heard and saw and who tells it.
Peter and Cornelius, told and then retold to the Church in Jerusalem.
Paul's own account of his visits to Jerusalem set beside Luke's account.
Two letters with a great deal of shared material, including the household codes.
Two letters that share a long section on false teachers. Scholars debate which depends on which.
Love of neighbour as the fulfilment of the law.
